claims.claim: Eustathius was a native of Side in Pamphylia.
He was bishop of Beroea (modern Aleppo) around 320 before becoming patriarch of Antioch shortly before or around 324/325.
He was bishop of Antioch from approximately 324 to 327/330.
He died in exile at Trajanopolis in Thrace, most probably around 360 according to some sources, though other sources suggest 336 or 337.
From 325-330 he was engaged in almost continuous literary warfare against the Arians.
He was deposed by a synod at Antioch in 327-328 or 330, accused of Sabellianism by suborned witnesses, and the deposition was confirmed by Emperor Constantine.
The work Contra Arianos was in eight books, and only fragments survive.
A critical edition of all surviving works was published by José H. Declerck in 2002 as Eustathii Antiocheni, Patris Nicaeni, opera quae supersunt omnia in the Corpus Christianorum Series Graeca 51.
Eustathius matters because he was one of the most prominent opponents of Arianism at the Council of Nicaea and significantly influenced the formulation of the Nicene Creed.
